## Context

When using the `OneToOneAssociationField` & `ManyToOneAssociationField` associations it is possible to specify the parameter `autoload` as `true`. This causes the association to be loaded with every query, regardless of whether the data is used or not.

This is a performance issue due to unnecessary data transfer, it slows down SQL queries with extra joins, slows the application down with hydrating and data processing and finally, API payloads are larger than they need to be.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

We will remove the `autoload` parameter from the constructor of `OneToOneAssociationField` & `ManyToOneAssociationField`.
The associations will no longer be loaded by default, regardless of whether the `autoload` parameter is set to true or not.

The only way to load these associations will be to explicitly request them in the criteria using `criteria.addAssociation()`.

This will lead to a performance improvement as unnecessary data transfer, SQL joins, hydration, and data processing are avoided. API payloads will also be smaller.

**Reasoning:**

*   **Explicit is better than implicit:** Requiring explicit association loading makes the data dependencies clear and prevents unintended performance bottlenecks.
*   **Performance:** Unnecessary joins and data processing are a significant performance drain, especially in large-scale applications.
*   **API Payload Size:** Smaller payloads reduce network traffic and improve responsiveness for API consumers.
*   **Consistency:** This aligns with the general best practice of loading only the data that is truly needed.

**Backward Compatibility Impact:**

*   **Breaking Change:** This is a breaking change. Any existing code that relies on `autoload=true` for `OneToOneAssociationField` or `ManyToOneAssociationField` will need to be updated to explicitly add the association to the criteria.

**Mitigation for Breaking Change:**

*   **Documentation:** Clear documentation will be provided to inform developers about this change and how to adapt their code.
*   **Deprecation Warning (if applicable):** If possible, a deprecation warning could be introduced in a minor version before the full removal in a major version to give developers time to adapt. However, given the immediate performance benefits, a direct removal might be preferred.

## Context
Currently, our ADRs are grouped into folders according to different areas. We have added this structure to help people find their way around when they are looking for specific ADRs.

However, there are different approaches when searching for ADRs:
1) I am looking for an ADR and I know the headline.
2) I would like to read the latest ADRs
3) I would like to see ADRs for a specific area.
4) ...

The structuring by areas is good for case 3, but not for the other two. In the first case, the user can easily use the search via the directory to use the appropriate ADR, but will also get duplicate matches. Depending on the keyword the result can be quite long.

In the second case, I would like to read the latest ADRs, the user would have to go to git history, which is only possible via shell or IDE.
decision:
## Decision
## Decision

We have decided to move all ADR files from their respective subfolders to the root of the ADR directory.

To facilitate navigation and information retrieval, we will introduce a new "Index" ADR (or "Overview" ADR). This Index ADR will contain a comprehensive, organized list of all other ADRs. The organization within the Index ADR will cater to various use cases for searching and browsing:

1.  **Chronological Order:** The Index ADR will list all ADRs in reverse chronological order (newest first) to easily identify the latest decisions. Each entry will include the ADR's title and a brief summary.
2.  **Categorization by Area:** The Index ADR will include a section that groups ADRs by the previously used "areas" or relevant domains. Each area will list the ADRs belonging to it.
3.  **Tags/Keywords:** The Index ADR will include a section or an integrated tagging system that allows ADRs to be easily discoverable via keywords.
4.  **Full-Text Search:** Users can leverage the built-text search capabilities of their IDE or file system for keyword-based searches across all ADR files, including the Index ADR. This addresses the "I know the headline" scenario more directly.

**Rationale:**

*   **Improved Discoverability for Latest ADRs:** Listing ADRs chronologically in the Index ADR provides a quick and accessible way to see recent decisions without needing to consult Git history.
*   **Centralized Overview:** The Index ADR acts as a single point of entry and reference, reducing the need to navigate through a deeply nested directory structure.
*   **Flexibility in Organization:** The Index ADR allows for multiple ways of organizing and presenting ADRs (chronological, categorical, tagged) without physically moving the files.
*   **Simplified File Structure:** A flat file structure (all ADRs in the root) makes it easier to manage files, perform bulk operations, and avoids potential conflicts related to directory changes.
*   **Enhanced Search Experience:** While individual ADRs are still searchable, the Index ADR provides curated lists that guide users, especially when they are exploring or trying to understand a specific domain.

## Decision

We will remove the area structure on directory level and introduce front matter in our ADRs as we already do in our changelog files. This makes it possible to extract metadata from content. Additionally, it can be used as groundwork, if we want to release our ADRs in different front-ends (handbook, dev-docs) and use the front-end's search functionalities.
With front matter and the flat file structure, you can solve all three problems described in this ADR. An example of this specific ADR would be:

## Context

The actions in Flow Builder are listening for Business Events. We want to implement the flow DelayAction in Flow Builder,
that means the actions can be delayed, and will be executed after  a set amount of time.
But we have some problems after the action was delayed:
* Events may contain old data, that data may be updated during the delay, and currently we don't have any way to restore
    the data.
* After a delay the rules have to be re-evaluated, but the data in the rules could be outdated or changed, so the rules
    have to be reloaded as well. Or the rules do not exist anymore.
decision:
## Decision
## Decision

To address the challenges of outdated data and rule re-evaluation after a `DelayAction` in Flow Builder, we will implement the following:

1.  **Event Data Refresh Strategy:**
    *   **Identify the Root Entity:** For each business event, determine the primary entity (or set of entities) that the event data represents. This will typically be the entity whose state is most critical for the delayed actions.
    *   **Store Entity Identifiers:** When a `DelayAction` is initiated, instead of storing the entire event payload, we will store the **identifiers** (e.g., UUIDs) of the root entities involved in the event. This prevents holding onto potentially stale data.
    *   **Re-hydrate Data on Execution:** When the `DelayAction`'s delay period expires and the subsequent actions are to be executed:
        *   The system will use the stored entity identifiers to fetch the *latest* state of those entities from the database.
        *   This fresh data will then be used to construct a new, up-to-date event payload for the delayed actions.
    *   **Handle Missing Entities:** If an entity identified by a stored ID no longer exists (e.g., it was deleted during the delay), the system should have a defined failure or skip strategy for the subsequent actions, logging the issue appropriately.

2.  **Rule Re-evaluation and Reloading:**
    *   **Store Rule Identifiers:** Similar to event data, when a `DelayAction` is initiated and rules are associated with the subsequent actions, we will store the **identifiers** of those rules (e.g., Rule IDs).
    *   **Re-evaluate Rules with Latest Data:** When the `DelayAction`'s delay period expires and the subsequent actions are to be executed:
        *   The system will fetch the *latest* version of the identified rules from the rule management system.
        *   The rules will then be re-evaluated using the *freshly re-hydrated event data* obtained from the Event Data Refresh Strategy (point 1).
    *   **Handle Deleted/Invalidated Rules:**
        *   If a rule identified by a stored ID no longer exists or has been marked as invalid, the system should treat that specific rule as no longer applicable. Depending on the flow's logic, this might mean skipping actions dependent on that rule or continuing with other valid rules.
        *   Implement robust logging to alert administrators about rules that become invalid or are deleted during a delay period.
    *   **Rule Versioning (Future Consideration):** For more advanced scenarios, consider implementing rule versioning. If a rule's definition changes significantly, the system could optionally enforce re-evaluation against a specific *version* of the rule that was active when the delay was initiated, or always use the *latest* version based on flow configuration. For the initial implementation, always using the latest version of the rule is sufficient.

This approach ensures that delayed actions operate on the most current state of the system and rules, minimizing the impact of data and rule changes during the delay period.

## Context
At the moment we have a bunch of different `FlowStorer` implementations. Most of them are used to store scalar values without any restore logic. Each of the Storer class has an own interface which is used to identify if the data of the event should be stored. This leads to much boilerplate code when adding new storer implementations or when plugins want to bypass some for events.
decision:
## Decision

### Decision

1.  **Introduce a Generic `FlowStorer` Interface:**
    Define a single, generic `FlowStorer` interface that can handle various types of data without requiring specific scalar value methods. This interface should provide methods for `store(key, value)` and `retrieve(key)` (or similar).

2.  **Standardize Event Data Structure for Storage:**
    Events that intend to be stored should contain a standardized data structure (e.g., a map or a dedicated DTO) that encapsulates the data to be persisted. This eliminates the need for each `FlowStorer` implementation to define its own interface for identifying data.

3.  **Implement a `StoreService` (or `FlowStoreManager`):**
    Create a central service responsible for orchestrating storage. This service would:
    *   Inject all available `FlowStorer` implementations.
    *   Receive events and the data they wish to store.
    *   Determine (via configuration or an event-specific flag/interface) which `FlowStorer` implementations are relevant for a given event and its data.
    *   Delegate the storage operation to the appropriate `FlowStorer(s)`.

4.  **Simplify Plugin Integration:**
    Plugins can register their custom `FlowStorer` implementations with the `StoreService`. To bypass storage for specific events, they can configure the `StoreService` or modify the event's data structure to indicate that it should not be stored by certain storers.

5.  **Refactor Existing `FlowStorer` Implementations:**
    Rewrite existing `FlowStorer` implementations to conform to the new generic interface and utilize the `StoreService`.

### Rationale

*   **Reduced Boilerplate:** A single generic `FlowStorer` interface and a central `StoreService` dramatically reduce the need for repetitive interface definitions and logic across multiple storer implementations.
*   **Improved Extensibility:** Adding new storer implementations becomes much simpler, as they only need to implement the generic interface and be registered with the `StoreService`.
*   **Easier Plugin Development:** Plugins can more easily integrate custom storage logic or control existing storage behaviors without deep modifications to core event handling.
*   **Centralized Control:** The `StoreService` provides a single point of control for managing storage concerns, making it easier to audit, configure, and troubleshoot.
*   **Clearer Responsibility:** Separating the concerns of *what* to store (event data structure), *how* to store (generic `FlowStorer`), and *who* stores it ( `StoreService`) leads to a more maintainable architecture.
*   **Decoupling:** Events no longer directly "know" about specific `FlowStorer` types; they simply provide data that *can* be stored, and the `StoreService` handles the storage logistics.

## Context
The current sw-text-editor in the administration has numerous low-level bugs in basic WYSIWYG features. It is built in a
way that is difficult to maintain and understand. Therefore, we require a new text editor that is easy to maintain, has
a good feature set, is flexible to extend and more stable.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision
For the new administration text editor, we will migrate from sw-text-editor to [TipTap v2](https://www.tiptap.dev/) for
the following reasons:

*   TipTap is a wrapper around [ProseMirror](https://prosemirror.net/), which handles a lot of the low-level editor-related bugs and quirks.
*   TipTap has a very good extension system. The most basic text editor functionality is split into multiple small
    extensions. We can add more extensions from the TipTap ecosystem or build custom extensions for our needs.
*   TipTap is framework agnostic. This means we can integrate it into our Vue 2 applications but it's also prepared
    for a future Vue 3 migration.
*   TipTap uses the [MIT license](https://github.com/ueberdosis/tiptap/blob/main/LICENSE) and is free to use.
predicted_decision:
## Decision
Building a new text editor from scratch is not a viable option. Therefore, we have evaluated various existing text 
editors and narrowed down our options to the following:

    - CKEditor 5
    - TinyMCE
    - QuillJS
    - Prosemirror
    - TipTap V2
    - Lexical

We have decided to skip CKEditor 5 and TinyMCE because they require a license for our use case and are not 100% open
source. Prosemirror was also ruled out because it provides only a low-level API and requires much more implementation 
time than the other editors. Additionally, Lexical is not a valid option for us since it is specialized for React 
environments and has no official support for VueJS.

The remaining two editors are TipTap V2 and QuillJS. Both have similar feature sets and APIs, but we have found some 
major differences between them. The first difference is that TipTap is a headless editor, which means that it only
provides the editor logic and requires a UI implementation. QuillJS, on the other hand, is a fully featured editor that
provides a UI out of the box. In our case, it is better to use a headless editor like TipTap because we can implement 
the UI to fit our needs, especially for several edge cases that are hard to implement in QuillJS.

The second major difference is in extensibility. TipTap's API is more flexible, allowing us to implement our own
features using the existing TipTap and ProseMirror plugins or build our own plugins. In most cases, the powerful main
TipTap API can already solve most of our use cases. QuillJS, on the other hand, is not as flexible as TipTap, and its
extension system is more complicated to use.

The third big difference is in stability. We found that TipTap is more stable than QuillJS, probably because TipTap is 
built on top of ProseMirror, which is a very stable and well-tested editor. Although QuillJS is also generally stable,
other developers have reported some issues with it in the past.

Our main decision driver was the extensibility of the editor. We want a text editor that is easy to extend and allows us
to implement our own features. TipTap provides a powerful extension system that is easy to use, and we can implement our
design without overwriting an existing design of other editors. Therefore, we have decided to use TipTap as the base of
our new text editor.

The current implementation of the salutation in Shopware 6 needs to handle cases where the salutation is not specified by the customer or administrator. To address this requirement and promote inclusivity, we have updated the default salutation to "not_specified" for unspecified salutations in our Shopware 6 platform.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

The default salutation for unspecified salutations in Shopware 6 will be updated to "not_specified".
This will ensure that the system handles cases where the salutation is not explicitly provided by the customer or administrator, promoting inclusivity and a consistent user experience.

This change will primarily impact areas of the platform where salutations are displayed or processed, such as:

*   **Customer registration forms:** If no salutation is chosen, "not_specified" will be the default.
*   **Customer profiles:** Existing customers with no specified salutation will display "not_specified".
*   **Communication templates (emails, documents):** Placeholder for salutation will render "not_specified" if the actual salutation is missing.
*   **API responses:** When retrieving customer data, the `salutation` field will return "not_specified" if not otherwise set.

**Implementation details:**

*   A new default salutation entity with the technical name "not_specified" will be added to the database during installation or update.
*   Relevant application logic will be updated to use "not_specified" as the fallback when a salutation is null or empty.
*   The "not_specified" salutation should be translatable to allow for appropriate display in different languages.
*   User interfaces (e.g., in the administration panel) that allow selecting salutations should offer "not_specified" as an option, possibly labeled as "Prefer not to say" or "No salutation".

## Context

The storefront CSS, compiled by `scssphp/scssphp`, is currently automatically prefixed with vendor prefixes using `padaliyajay/php-autoprefixer`.
However, the generated prefixes no longer add much value since the browser support has been updated with the Bootstrap v5 update.
Most of the prefixes are unnecessary for the supported browsers in .browserslist.
Unfortunately, the `theme:compile` process experiences a significant decrease in performance due to the auto-prefixer, which is particularly problematic in our SaaS solution.
Moreover, the `padaliyajay/php-autoprefixer` package does not work dynamically and fails to consider `.browserslist` while applying the appropriate vendor-prefixes.
This package hard-codes the CSS properties that require prefixing, making it an unsustainable long-term solution.
To demonstrate this, a table containing all automatic prefixes generated by `padaliyajay/php-autoprefixer` is provided below.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

The `padaliyajay/php-autoprefixer` package will be removed.

**Consequences:**

* The `theme:compile` process will no longer be slowed down by the auto-prefixer, resulting in a significant performance improvement.
* The CSS output will be slightly smaller due to the removal of unnecessary prefixes.
* We rely on the fact that Bootstrap 5, together with our supported browsers, already accounts for most of the necessary prefixes.
* If a prefix is still required for a specific property, it must be added manually. This can be done by using a custom PostCSS pipeline or by directly adding the prefixed property to the SCSS.
* The `scssphp/scssphp` compiler only processes standard CSS and does not automatically add vendor prefixes.
* While we are removing this auto-prefixing step, we acknowledge that a more robust and dynamic solution like PostCSS with Autoprefixer could be beneficial in the future if browser support requirements change or if we introduce more experimental CSS features. However, for the current supported browser list, this manual prefixing is deemed acceptable.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

* Due to the above points we have decided to disable the CSS auto-prefixing by default.
* In case it is still needed, to support older browsers or some special CSS property from the table above, it can still be activated via the config key `storefront.theme.auto_prefix_css` in `Storefront/Resources/config/packages/storefront.yaml`. However, we recommend to do a manual prefix inside the SCSS instead.
* We will deprecate the auto-prefixing for v6.6.0 and only use SCSS compiling
* We do not consider the deactivation of the auto-prefixing as a hard breaking change because:
    * Most prefixes are not needed due to current browser support.
    * Some prefixes are for CSS properties which are no longer implemented and developed by browsers.
    * Prefixes which are still valid are primarily cosmetic/appearance properties which are very unlikely to affect the Storefronts functionality.

## Context
A pre-release package version is a version followed by a hyphen and an alphanumeric string.

Imagine the following scenario:
* An imaginary package is marked as insecure with version 1.8.7
* The issue is fixed with 2.0.0
* We use version `1.9.0-alpha1`
* Any pre-release package version like `1.9.0-alpha1` is interpreted as `<0.0.0` by npm

Why is this problematic?

The insecurity introduced with version `1.8.7` would never get reported to us by npm, unless we switch to a none pre-release version.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

This means that a version `1.9.0-alpha1` is evaluated by npm as being smaller than `1.8.7`, therefore the `1.8.7` is never matched, and so never flagged as insecure.

This means that, if the security team marks `1.8.7` as insecure and the fix is `2.0.0`, but we are using `1.9.0-alpha1`, we don't get a report, because npm thinks `1.9.0-alpha1` is smaller than `1.8.7`.

We will therefore change our dependency management. We will avoid the use of pre-release versions for dependencies.
We only use full versions in our `package.json` with the `~` operator (e.g., `~1.9.0`), which will only update patch versions.
This will allow us to get security updates, as it will be correctly evaluated by npm.
If the project needs to upgrade to a newer version (e.g., `2.0.0`), we will do so manually.
predicted_decision:
## Decision
Using pre-release package versions is prohibited.
This will be checked via a npm `preinstall` script.

## Context

The existing SQL snippet to delete the outdated cart entries doesn't use any database index to narrow down entries that can be deleted. 
On high traffic shops this leads to SQL query times larger than 30 seconds to find and remove these database entries.

Running 
```
EXPLAIN DELETE FROM cart
WHERE (updated_at IS NULL AND created_at <= '2023-02-01')
   OR (updated_at IS NOT NULL AND updated_at <= '2023-02-01') LIMIT 1000;
```
shows that the original sql query doesn't use an index (`possible_keys` = `NULL`)
decision:
## Decision
We should create an index on the `updated_at` and `created_at` columns of the `cart` table.
Specifically, a composite index covering both `updated_at` and `created_at` might be beneficial, or separate indexes if the query optimizer can effectively use them.

**Proposed Index:**

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_cart_updated_created_at ON cart (updated_at, created_at);
```

**Explanation:**

*   **`idx_cart_updated_created_at`**: This name clearly indicates the columns involved in the index.
*   **`(updated_at, created_at)`**: This creates a composite index. The order of columns in the index is important. In this case, `updated_at` is likely to be more selective for the `OR` condition, so it's placed first. If `updated_at` is `NULL`, `created_at` will be used. A composite index can cover both parts of the `OR` condition more efficiently than separate indexes in some scenarios, especially when the optimizer can perform index merges or use one index and then filter with the other.

**Alternative (if the composite index isn't fully utilized):**

If the database optimizer struggles with the `OR` condition using a single composite index, creating two separate indexes might be considered, though it increases write overhead:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_cart_updated_at ON cart (updated_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_cart_created_at ON cart (created_at);
```

However, the composite index is generally preferred first to minimize index storage and maintenance overhead. The database optimizer is often intelligent enough to use parts of a composite index.

**Expected Outcome:**

After creating the index, the `EXPLAIN` output for the `DELETE` query should show that `idx_cart_updated_created_at` (or the individual indexes) is being used in `possible_keys` and likely in `key`, leading to a significant reduction in query execution time for finding and deleting outdated cart entries. The `LIMIT 1000` will then operate on an already narrowed-down set of candidates, further improving performance.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

Reorder the query parameters so that the relevant cart entries can be narrowed down by an indexed field.

Testing the new SQL snippet by running 
```
EXPLAIN DELETE FROM cart
        WHERE created_at <= '2023-02-01'
          AND (updated_at IS NULL OR updated_at <= '2023-02-01') LIMIT 1000;
```
shows that the new query uses an index (`possible_keys` = `idx.cart.created_at`).

## Context

Currently, it is hard to publish features in an early state to gather feedback regarding those features. If they are useful, what needs to be improved etc.
One major reason is that everything we publish (that is not marked as internal) is part of our backwards compatibility promise, thus changing foundational parts of features is quite hard after first release.
That leads to features being developed over quite some time without getting actual feedback from users or being able to release them, as they need to be implemented to a pretty final state in order to confidently release them in a stable manner, where we will keep backwards compatibility.

This at the same time also means that the current approach is not beneficial to our ecosystem, whom the whole backwards compatibility promise should benefit, because the features are built behind closed curtains they can't chime in with ideas and use cases regarding extendability, etc.

Examples of features that could benefit from an earlier experimental release:
* B2B:
  * We could release the multi account B2B feature with a "simple" employee management system first, and then add the more complex budget management or access control on top of that later.
* Advanced Search:

Experimental features are features that are still under development and might change in the future. They are not part of our backwards compatibility promise.

## Context

The stock handling in Shopware 6 is currently not very flexible and does not support many common use cases. 

* It's not possible to easily replace the loading of stocks with a custom implementation, for example one that communicates with an ERP.
* It's not possible to easily modify how stock is increased/decreased throughout the order lifecycle.
* Available stock calculation is very slow on large catalogs.
* Stock is stored as two distinct values: stock and available stock. This is due to the fact that stock is not reduced until an order is set as completed. Therefore, the available stock is calculated as the stock minus all open orders. This is unnecessarily complex.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

The following changes will be made to improve flexibility and performance:

**1. Stock is solely represented by one value: `stock`**

* The `available_stock` column will be removed from the `product` table.
* The `stock` column in the `product` table will represent the actual physical stock.
* When a product is added to an order (e.g., in a "pending" or "open" state), the `stock` will be immediately reduced.
* When an order is cancelled or a return is processed, the `stock` will be increased accordingly.
* This simplifies stock management and eliminates the need for complex calculations of available stock.

**2. Introduction of a `StockUpdater` service**

* A new service, `StockUpdater`, will be introduced.
* This service will be responsible for all operations that modify the `stock` of a product (e.g., increasing, decreasing, setting).
* The `StockUpdater` will expose public methods for these operations.
* This service will be designed to be easily extensible, allowing for custom implementations to replace or augment its behavior.
* **Example Use Cases for Extensibility:**
    * **ERP Integration:** A plugin could replace the `StockUpdater` to communicate stock changes to an external ERP system, rather than directly modifying the Shopware database.
    * **Advanced Stock Logic:** A plugin could introduce custom logic for stock allocation, reservations, or backorders by extending the `StockUpdater`.
    * **Logging/Auditing:** All stock changes could be logged for auditing purposes by decorating the `StockUpdater`.

**3. Event-driven Stock Changes**

* All actions that trigger stock changes (e.g., order placement, order cancellation, product returns) will dispatch events.
* The `StockUpdater` will listen to these events and perform the necessary stock modifications.
* This decouples the stock management from the business logic of various modules, making the system more modular and maintainable.
* **Example Events:**
    * `OrderPlacedEvent`: Triggers a stock decrease for ordered products.
    * `OrderCancelledEvent`: Triggers a stock increase for cancelled products.
    * `OrderLineItemReturnedEvent`: Triggers a stock increase for returned products.

**4. Optimized Stock Loading**

* The current slow stock loading mechanism will be replaced with a more efficient approach.
* For simple stock availability checks (e.g., "is product in stock?"), a direct database query will be used to retrieve the `stock` value.
* For more complex scenarios (e.g., retrieving stock for multiple products, filtering by stock status), an optimized query builder or a dedicated repository will be introduced to fetch stock information efficiently.
* Caching mechanisms will be implemented to further improve the performance of stock loading for frequently accessed products.

**Benefits of this Decision:**

* **Increased Flexibility:** The `StockUpdater` service and event-driven approach allow for easy customization and integration with external systems (e.g., ERP).
* **Simplified Stock Management:** Consolidating stock into a single `stock` value reduces complexity and potential for inconsistencies.
* **Improved Performance:** Optimized stock loading and caching will significantly improve the performance of stock-related operations, especially for large catalogs.
* **Better Maintainability:** Decoupling stock management from business logic makes the system more modular and easier to understand and maintain.

By default, every exception that is thrown in the PHP stack and not caught will be logged by the `symfony/monolog-bridge` on `error` level.
But there are some cases where the exception is caused by clients accessing the API wrong (missing fields etc.) and throwing an `ShopwareHttpException` with an HTTP-Status-Code of 40x is our way of handling such situations and returning a correct HTTP-Status-Code to the client.
So those cases are in fact no "errors" that need to be analyzed, but are expected given a malformed API request.
Logging those cases as "errors" produces a lot of noise, which makes it harder to actually find errors in the logs.

decision:
## Decision

We will add a configuration parameter that allows configuring which exceptions should not be logged as errors.
This configuration parameter will be an array of exception class names. If an exception is an instance of one of the configured classes, it will be logged at the `notice` level instead of the `error` level.

We will provide a default configuration for this parameter that includes `ShopwareHttpException` and its subclasses. This will ensure that common client errors are not logged as errors by default.

This approach offers the following benefits:

*   **Reduces log noise:** By demoting expected client errors to `notice` level, we reduce the amount of "error" logs, making it easier to identify genuine application errors.
*   **Maintainability:** The configuration is centralized and easy to manage.
*   **Flexibility:** Users can extend or modify the list of exceptions that should be logged as `notice` to suit their specific needs.
*   **Consistency:** Aligns with the existing practice in the cloud product.

## Context

Using UUIDs as primary keys eases the integration of several different data sources,
but it also brings some performance issues.

Currently, we're using UUIDv4, which is a random UUID the completely random prefix means
that the B-tree indexes of the database are not very efficient.

UUIDv7 time-based prefix is less spread than that of UUIDv4, this helps the database to keep the index more compact.
It allows the Index to allocate fewer new pages and to keep the index smaller.
decision:
## Decision
## Decision

We propose using UUIDv7 as the primary key. This will improve the performance of our database by reducing index fragmentation and making B-tree indexes more efficient. While UUIDv4 offers a high degree of randomness, its lack of an ordered prefix leads to significant performance degradation in database systems, particularly with large datasets and frequent inserts. UUIDv7, with its time-based prefix, offers a superior alternative by providing a more sequential and compact index, thereby reducing the need for new page allocations and keeping the index smaller. This change will lead to faster data retrieval and improved overall database performance.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

Considering there is little risk to using UUIDv7, as v4 and v7 share the same
length and are indistinguishable for shopware, we can switch to v7 without any risk
of breaking anything.

The effort is also very low as we only need to change the
implementation of the `Uuid` class. As using UUIDv7 will improve the speed of
bulk product inserts by about 8 %, we think the effort is worth the measurable and
theoretical gain.

## Context

Right now only Shopware Backend is able to communicate with the App Server in a secure way.
This is because the App Server is able to verify the origin of the request by checking request signature, 
and this signature is generated by the Shopware 6 backend application with a shop to app server secret.

When an app wants to communicate directly with the App Server,
the App Server is not able to verify the origin of the request and has to trust the client.
This works fine for public available data, but not when you reliably need the logged-in customer and other information.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

Shopware will introduce a new authentication method for the App Server.
The App Server will be able to verify the origin of the request by checking a request signature.
This signature will be generated by the Shopware 6 frontend application (Storefront or Headless) with a public/private key pair.

When an app wants to communicate directly with the App Server,
the App Server will be able to verify the origin of the request by checking the request signature.
The signature will be generated by the app with the private key, and the App Server will verify it with the public key.

This new authentication method will allow apps to communicate directly with the App Server in a secure way,
and will also allow the App Server to reliably identify the logged-in customer and other information.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

We provide a new endpoint `/store-api/app-system/{appName}/generate-token` (`/app-system/{appName}/generate-token` in Storefront) which generates a JWT token for the given app.
This endpoint requires that the customer is logged-in and the app is installed and active. 

The JWT token contains claims like:
- `iat` - issued at
- `exp` - expiration time
- `shopId` - the shop id of the current shop
- `salesChannelId` - the sales channel id of the current sales channel
- `customerId` - the customer id of the logged-in customer
- `cartToken` - the cart token of the current cart

The additional claims are bound to app permissions when an app does not have permissions to read a customer,
it does not get the `customerId` claim.

The JWT token is signed with the shop to app server secret key which we use already for the signature.
So the App Server needs to be able to verify the JWT key and use the claims in a secure way.
The request body of the client is still untrusted and has to be properly validated by the app server.

The request cycle would look like this:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Shopware Backend
    participant App Server
    Client->>Shopware Backend: GET /store-api/app-system/TestApp/generate-token
    Shopware Backend->>Client: Responds with Signed JWT Token
    Client->>App Server: Post /product-review/submit containing JWT in header
```

The JWT token is valid for 15 minutes and can be used multiple times until expired.
The client should save it in the [session storage](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/sessionStorage)
and request it only on expiry again.
Additionally, the API route should be rate limited to not generate too often an expensive JWT key.

## Context
Our current development process uses ['Experimental features'](./2023-05-10-experimental-features.md) to publish features in an early state to gather feedback regarding those features.
During the implementation, developers may encounter challenges related to the effective management of extensive code scattered throughout the platform, particularly in connection with specific experimental features. This codebase fragmentation presents impediments to the tracking, maintenance, and comprehensive understanding of each feature's scope, thereby hindering our development progress.
 
Potential problems:
* Update `stableVersion` property for Prolonged Experiments
    * When a decision is made to extend an experiment, locating all relevant sections of code for updating the property `stableVersion` in `@experimental` annotation becomes a cumbersome task.
* Deprecation of Killed Features
    * Identifying and marking as deprecated the components associated with a deprecated experimental feature is problematic, particularly when multiple experimental features coexist simultaneously within the platform.
    * The ['Experimental features'](./2023-05-10-experimental-features.md) stipulates the "Killing Feature" rule, which mandates that a feature must remain within the platform's codebase until the next major version and be appropriately marked as deprecated. However, it is hardly possible to check with current annotation.

In all the above case main problem is detection to which feature belongs experimental code.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

We will implement a system that categorizes experimental code by feature. Instead of directly using annotations like `@experimental`, we will introduce a mechanism that groups all code related to an experimental feature under a common identifier.

**Proposed Solution:**

1.  **Feature Flag Definition:**
    *   Each experimental feature will have a unique, short, and descriptive identifier (e.g., `featureA`, `newCheckout`, `aiAssistant`).
    *   This identifier will be defined in a central configuration or an enumeration of available experimental features.

2.  **Code Grouping Mechanism:**
    *   **Dedicated Folders/Namespaces:** For larger features, all related files (classes, templates, configuration) will reside in a dedicated folder or namespace, prefixed with the feature identifier (e.g., `src/Core/FeatureA/`, `src/Storefront/Controller/NewCheckoutController.php`).
    *   **Conditional Code Blocks:** For smaller changes or integrations into existing code, we will use explicit feature flags in conditional statements. Instead of `if ($this->isExperimental())`, we will use `if (Feature::isActive('featureA'))`. The `Feature` class will centralize the logic for checking feature status.
    *   **Annotation with Feature Identifier:** If annotations are still deemed necessary (e.g., for marking entire classes or methods), they will include the feature identifier directly: `@experimental(feature="featureA")`.

3.  **Centralized Feature Status Management:**
    *   A single point of truth (e.g., a `FeatureManager` service or a `features.yaml` configuration file) will manage the status of all experimental features (enabled/disabled, stable version, deprecation status).

**How this addresses the problems:**

*   **Update `stableVersion` property for Prolonged Experiments:**
    *   With code grouped by feature identifier, updating `stableVersion` (or any other lifecycle property) becomes a matter of updating the central feature definition for `featureA`, rather than searching scattered annotations. Tools could even be developed to lint or automatically update these definitions.

*   **Deprecation of Killed Features:**
    *   When `featureA` is "killed," its status in the central `FeatureManager` can be set to "deprecated."
    *   All code that uses `Feature::isActive('featureA')` will automatically respect this new status.
    *   The dedicated folders/namespaces for `featureA` make it trivial to identify all related files for removal or specific deprecation marking (e.g., adding a `@deprecated` annotation to an entire class within `src/Core/FeatureA/`).
    *   Automated scripts could identify files within `src/Core/FeatureA/` and flag them for deprecation or removal based on the central feature status.

*   **Improved Detection and Tracking:**
    *   Developers can quickly grasp the scope of an experimental feature by looking at its dedicated folder or searching for its unique identifier (`featureA`).
    *   It simplifies code reviews and ensures that all parts of an experiment are considered together.
    *   Makes it easier to develop tooling for analyzing experimental feature usage and lifecycle.

## Context
For our ambitions to consequently reduce manual testing in favour for test automation the current E2E test suite, based on Cypress, is not sufficient anymore. It has several flaws that have become a big road-blocker. The test suite is tightly coupled to the state of the test environment, which leads to tests that are not very deterministic and tend to be slow and flaky. Tests are often created in different ways and don't follow a specific strategy. In addition, the test suite is currently not able to test against our cloud environment.

Our goal is to create a test suite that fulfills the following requirements:

*  Deterministic tests that can run against any environment.
*  Fast and reliable tests that follow a certain test strategy.
*  Tests that are derived from real product requirements and validate behaviour.
*  A test framework that is easy to learn and using a readable syntax that also non-tech people can comprehend.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

The new E2E test suite will be based on Playwright and TypeScript.

The test suite will follow a BDD-style approach and use a page object model for better maintainability and readability. The tests will be written in a way that they are independent of the environment and can be run against any environment (local, staging, production, cloud).

To achieve this, the tests will:

*   **Be self-contained:** Each test will create its own test data and clean it up afterwards, ensuring a consistent test environment.

## Context
1. If flow actions want to interact with the database in a transactional manner, they need to handle it themselves by starting and committing transactions.

2. When there is a problem committing the transaction, the error will be caught and ignored by the flow dispatcher. A vague error message will be logged, but the flows will continue to execute.
This is problematic if a transaction was already started before the flow is executed. If the connection is configured without save points (which is the default with Shopware), when a nested commit fails (eg during a flow action) the connection will be marked as rollback only.
When the outer transaction attempts to commit, eg the calling code, it will be unaware of the previous inner commit failure and thus will also fail.
decision:
## Decision
## Decision

We have a number of ways to address this issue:

1. **Let flows handle their own transactions completely.**
    * **Pros:** Simplest implementation. Flow actions can interact with the database in a way that aligns with their specific needs (e.g., read-only, multiple independent transactions within a flow action).
    * **Cons:**
        * Requires every flow action that modifies the database to explicitly start, commit, and rollback its own transactions. This is boilerplate and prone to errors (e.g., forgetting a `rollback` on failure).
        * Lack of atomicity across multiple flow actions within a single flow if they are intended to be part of a larger, coordinated operation.
        * The "outer transaction" issue still exists if flow actions are called within an existing transaction.
        * The "vague error message" issue would still exist for transactional failures within a flow action, unless each flow action implements robust error handling.

2. **Wrap each flow action in its own transaction within the flow dispatcher.**
    * **Pros:**
        * Each flow action's database interactions are atomic.
        * The flow dispatcher can catch transactional errors more specifically and provide clearer logging/error handling for individual action failures.
    * **Cons:**
        * If a flow consists of multiple actions that logically belong to a single, larger transaction (e.g., "create order" flow with separate actions for "create order record", "deduct stock", "send confirmation email"), this approach breaks that atomicity. If "deduct stock" fails, "create order record" would still be committed.
        * Potential for many small transactions, which can have performance implications.
        * Still doesn't inherently solve the "outer transaction" problem; if the flow is called within an existing transaction, the inner transaction from the flow action could still mark the outer transaction as rollback-only if it fails.

3. **Wrap the *entire flow execution* in a single transaction within the flow dispatcher.**
    * **Pros:**
        * Ensures that all database operations across all actions within a flow are atomic. If any action fails, the entire flow's database changes are rolled back. This is often the desired behavior for a "business process" flow.
        * Centralized transaction management within the flow dispatcher simplifies individual flow actions.
        * The "outer transaction" problem is directly addressed. If the flow dispatcher starts a transaction, it will handle committing or rolling back that transaction based on the flow's success or failure, independent of any calling code's transaction.
        * Clearer error handling for the entire flow.
    * **Cons:**
        * Some flow actions might not require transactional behavior, or might need to perform non-transactional operations (e.g., sending an external API request). These would still be rolled back if a later action fails, which might be undesirable.
        * Potentially long-running transactions if flows involve many steps or external calls, which can lead to locking issues or resource contention.
        * If a flow action *intends* to commit an intermediate state, this approach prevents it.

4. **Implement a hybrid approach: A default transaction for the entire flow, but allow flow actions to opt-out or manage sub-transactions.**
    * **Pros:**
        * Provides atomicity for the majority of flows by default.
        * Offers flexibility for advanced use cases where an action needs different transactional behavior.
        * Addresses the "outer transaction" problem and provides centralized error handling.
    * **Cons:**
        * More complex implementation in the flow dispatcher and for flow action developers.
        * Introduces an API for transactional control within flow actions.

**Decision:**

We will implement **Option 3: Wrap the entire flow execution in a single transaction within the flow dispatcher.**

This approach provides the strongest guarantee of data consistency for a "flow" as a logical unit of work. It directly addresses the issue of a failed inner commit marking an outer transaction as rollback-only, as the flow dispatcher will now manage its own top-level transaction. It also simplifies the development of individual flow actions, as they no longer need to explicitly manage transactions for their database interactions within the flow.

**Details:**

*   The `FlowDispatcher` will be responsible for starting a database transaction before executing any flow actions.
*   If all flow actions execute successfully, the transaction will be committed.
*   If any flow action (or any subsequent database operation within the flow) throws an exception, the transaction will be rolled back.
*   The `FlowDispatcher` will log a more specific error message in case of transaction commit/rollback failures.
*   Flow actions that need to interact with external services or perform operations that should *not* be rolled back (e.g., sending an email) should be designed to execute only *after* critical transactional database operations have been successfully committed, or be idempotent.

**Rationale for choosing Option 3 over other options:**

*   **1 (Flows handle their own transactions):** Too much boilerplate and error-prone. Fails to provide atomicity across multiple actions within a flow. Doesn't solve the core problem of outer transaction awareness.
*   **2 (Each action in its own transaction):** Breaks atomicity across a logical flow. While it addresses the specific commit failure for *that action*, it doesn't ensure the "all or nothing" nature often desired for a business flow. Still has the outer transaction issue for each individual action.
*   **4 (Hybrid):** While theoretically ideal for maximum flexibility, it adds significant complexity that may not be immediately necessary given the current context. A simpler, default-atomic approach (Option 3) should cover the majority of use cases and can be extended later if specific needs for sub-transactions arise. The current problem points to a need for stronger, default atomicity for the flow itself.

This decision prioritizes consistency and simplifies flow action development by centralizing transaction management at the flow level.

## Context

In our current architecture, we rely heavily on PHP decoration, Adapter, and Factory patterns to allow for extensions and customizations by third-party developers. While these patterns are effective, they present significant challenges:

1. **Backward and Forward Compatibility:**
    - Maintaining backward and forward compatibility with these patterns is complex and labor-intensive. Each change or update can potentially break existing extensions or require extensive rework to ensure compatibility.

2. **Process Extension Limitations:**
    - These patterns do not inherently allow for the extension of subprocesses unless these subprocesses are extracted into separate classes and interfaces. This extraction often results in a proliferation of interfaces, abstract classes, and their implementations.

3. **Proliferation of Code:**
    - The need to extract subprocesses into separate entities leads to an overwhelming number of interfaces and abstract classes. This proliferation makes the codebase more difficult to understand and maintain, and increases the cognitive load on developers.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

We will transition away from a heavy reliance on decoration, Adapter, and Factory patterns for extensibility. Instead, we will adopt a more modular and event-driven architecture that promotes better backward and forward compatibility and simplifies process extension.

Our new approach will focus on the following principles:

1.  **Event-Driven Architecture:**
    *   Introduce a robust event dispatcher system. All significant actions and state changes within the core system will emit events.
    *   Third-party developers can subscribe to these events to inject custom logic, modify data, or trigger side effects without directly altering core classes. This allows for non-invasive extensions and improves compatibility.

2.  **Service Interfaces and Implementations (without extensive decoration chains):**
    *   For core functionalities that require explicit replacement or alternative implementations, we will define clear service interfaces.
    *   The system will use a dependency injection container to resolve these services. Third-party developers can register their own implementations of these service interfaces (or register decorators directly if absolutely necessary for specific use cases), but the default expectation is a clear replacement rather than a deep decoration chain.

3.  **Plugin System for Subprocess Overrides:**
    *   Implement a dedicated plugin system or strategy pattern for extending or overriding specific subprocesses. Instead of extracting every subprocess into a new interface, we will define clear extension points where plugins can register their own logic. This could involve:
        *   **Strategy Pattern:** Define a base strategy interface for a process, and allow plugins to register alternative strategies.
        *   **Middleware/Pipeline Pattern:** For sequential processes, allow plugins to inject middleware that can modify input, execute logic, or short-circuit the process.
    *   This approach avoids the need for a separate interface/abstract class for every tiny subprocess, reducing code proliferation.

4.  **Configuration-Driven Extensibility:**
    *   Utilize configuration files (e.g., YAML, XML) to register extensions, event listeners, and custom service implementations. This provides a centralized and discoverable way for developers to customize the application.

5.  **Clear Documentation and Extension Guidelines:**
    *   Prioritize comprehensive documentation outlining official extension points, event contracts, and best practices for developing backward-compatible extensions.

**Rationale:**

*   **Improved Backward and Forward Compatibility:** Event-driven architecture inherently promotes looser coupling. Changes in core implementation details are less likely to break extensions as long as event contracts remain stable. New events can be added without affecting existing listeners.
*   **Simplified Process Extension:** The event system and a targeted plugin/strategy pattern reduce the need for excessive interfaces. Developers can react to or replace specific parts of a process without having to navigate deep inheritance or decoration hierarchies.
*   **Reduced Code Proliferation:** By minimizing the number of interfaces and abstract classes needed solely for extensibility, the codebase becomes leaner, easier to understand, and less intimidating for new developers.
*   **Clearer Extension Points:** Event definitions and explicit plugin interfaces make it much clearer where and how the system can be extended, compared to the implicit nature of deep decoration chains.

## Decision

To address these challenges, we have decided to transition to an event-based extension system. This new approach will replace the existing decoration, Adapter, and Factory patterns as the primary method for extending and customizing our system.

## Context

In some instances, a system rollout was completed where an error in certain system functionalities was not detected until the system was live.

A software system is made up of many components that work together to provide a service. The software system can still be healthy even if some of its components are not fully in a healthy state.  System health checks are a way to monitor the health of a system and detect failures early.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

We will implement health checks at both the system and component level.

**System Health Checks**

* **API Endpoint:** A dedicated `/health` API endpoint will be created for the overall system health check.
* **Aggregated Status:** This endpoint will aggregate the health status of critical system components.
* **Basic Reachability:** It will at minimum confirm that the application process is running and can respond to requests.
* **Database Connectivity:** It will check if the application can connect to its primary database.
* **External Service Connectivity:** It will verify connectivity to critical external services (e.g., message queues, external APIs).
* **Metrics:** The health check will report a simple UP/DOWN status and potentially include details about unhealthy components for debugging.
* **Monitoring Integration:** Monitoring tools (e.g., Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog) will be configured to periodically poll this endpoint and alert on failures.

**Component Health Checks**

* **Granular Monitoring:** Each significant component within the system (e.g., individual microservices, background workers, specific database connections) will have its own health check mechanism.
* **Component-Specific Logic:** These checks will include logic relevant to the component's function (e.g., database connection pool utilization, message queue backlog, CPU/memory usage for a specific service).
* **Internal Exposure:** These component health metrics will be exposed internally, typically via a metrics endpoint (e.g., `/metrics`) that monitoring systems can scrape.
* **Logging:** Failures or degraded states in component health checks will be logged with sufficient detail for diagnosis.
* **Alerting:** Alerts will be configured for critical component failures, potentially with different severity levels based on impact.

**Failure Handling and Reporting**

* **Graceful Degradation:** The system should be designed to continue operating, possibly with reduced functionality, even if some non-critical components are unhealthy.
* **Clear Error Messages:** Health check failures should provide clear, actionable error messages.
* **Downtime Minimization:** The goal is to detect issues before they cause widespread outages or significant customer impact.
* **Rollback Strategy:** In cases where new deployments introduce health issues, a clear rollback strategy will be in place.

**Implementation Details**

* **Framework Support:** Utilize built-in health check features of the chosen application framework (e.g., Spring Boot Actuator, ASP.NET Core Health Checks).
* **Custom Checks:** Implement custom health checks for business-critical logic or external dependencies not covered by standard framework features.
* **Regular Review:** Health check configurations and thresholds will be regularly reviewed and updated as the system evolves.

## Context

Our Vue.js application currently uses the Options API, which is the traditional way of writing Vue components in Vue 2. With the release of Vue 3, the Composition API was introduced, offering improved code organization, better TypeScript support, and enhanced reusability of component logic. For more detailed information about the reasons for migrating to the Composition API, see the [documentation entry](https://developer.shopware.com/docs/guides/plugins/plugins/administration/system-updates/vue-native.html).

To modernize our codebase and take advantage of these benefits, we need to migrate our existing Vue 2 Options API components to use the Vue 3 Composition API. Manual conversion of numerous components would be time-consuming and error-prone. Therefore, we need an automated solution to assist in this migration process.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

We will use a custom script to automate the migration of Vue 2 Options API components to the Vue 3 Composition API. This script will be developed as a one-off tool to assist with the transition, rather than a continuously maintained utility.

**Why a custom script?**

While external migration tools exist, they often come with a learning curve, may not perfectly align with our specific codebase conventions, or might introduce external dependencies we prefer to avoid for a one-time migration. A custom script allows us to:

*   **Target specific patterns:** Tailor the migration logic to our existing component structures and common patterns.
*   **Handle edge cases:** Address unique situations or complex components that generic tools might miss or misinterpret.
*   **Maintain control:** Have full control over the transformation process and the resulting code style.
*   **Avoid external dependencies:** Prevent adding new tools or libraries that would only be used for this migration and then become deprecated.

**How the script will work:**

The script will primarily focus on identifying common Options API patterns and converting them to their Composition API equivalents. This will include:

1.  **Data properties to `ref` or `reactive`:** Convert `data` properties into reactive references using `ref` for primitives and `reactive` for objects.
2.  **Computed properties to `computed`:** Transform `computed` properties into `computed` functions within the `setup` block.
3.  **Methods to functions:** Convert `methods` into standard JavaScript functions.
4.  **Watchers to `watch`:** Migrate `watch` options to the `watch` function.
5.  **Lifecycle hooks to `onMounted`, `onUpdated`, etc.:** Convert Options API lifecycle hooks to their Composition API equivalents.
6.  **Props to `defineProps`:** Migrate props definition to use `defineProps`.
7.  **Emits to `defineEmits`:** Migrate emit definitions to use `defineEmits`.
8.  **Setup function generation:** Encapsulate the transformed logic within a `setup` function that returns the exposed properties and methods.

**Limitations and Manual Review:**

While the script aims to automate a significant portion of the migration, it will not be able to cover every possible scenario or perfectly refactor complex logic. Therefore, a thorough **manual review of all migrated components will be mandatory.** This review will ensure:

*   **Correctness:** The transformed logic functions as expected.
*   **Performance:** No performance regressions are introduced.
*   **Best practices:** The code adheres to Composition API best practices and our internal coding standards.
*   **TypeScript inference:** Ensure correct TypeScript types are inferred or explicitly defined where necessary.
*   **Refactoring opportunities:** Identify and apply further refactoring to improve readability and reusability, which an automated script might not achieve.

This approach balances the efficiency of automation with the precision and quality control of manual human oversight.

## Context
The current block system relies on TwigJs for creating reusable and extendable component template.
This system allows plugin developers to override or extend content in predefined blocks using TwigJsÃÂÃÂ¡ÃÂÃÂ¯s inheritance mechanisms. Vue.js offers a more dynamic and reactive component-based architecture which is better suited for modern frontend development.

To replace TwigJs with a native Vue.js approach we need to introduce two new component `sw-block` and `sw-block-parent`.

The new `sw-block` and `sw-block-parent` components in Vue.js aim to replicate and improve on the TwigJs block system by providing a component-based approach. These components offer enhanced flexibility by allowing dynamic content overriding and extension directly in VueÃÂÃÂ¡ÃÂÃÂ¯s templating and reactivity model.
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision
We will replace TwigJs with a native Vue.js approach for our block system, leveraging two new components: `sw-block` and `sw-block-parent`.

The `sw-block` component will define a section of content that can be overridden or extended. It will take a `name` prop to identify the block uniquely. When rendered, it will check if any descendant `sw-block-parent` components (within an `sw-component-section` boundary) are attempting to extend or override it.

The `sw-block-parent` component will be used by plugin developers or child components to modify the content of a named `sw-block`. It will also take a `name` prop, corresponding to the `name` of the `sw-block` it intends to target.

**Key features and benefits of this approach:**

1.  **Dynamic Overriding and Extension:** Unlike TwigJs, which relies on static template inheritance, the Vue.js components will allow for dynamic modification of block content. This means blocks can be overridden or extended at runtime based on application state or user interactions.

2.  **Vue.js Reactivity:** The content within `sw-block` components will benefit from Vue.js's reactivity system. Any data changes within the component will automatically re-render the block content, providing a more dynamic and responsive user experience.

3.  **Component-Based Architecture:** Aligning with Vue.js principles, this system treats blocks as first-class components, making them easier to manage, test, and reuse within the Vue.js ecosystem.

4.  **Improved Developer Experience:** Developers will be able to leverage Vue.js's familiar templating syntax, props, slots, and reactivity model to define and modify blocks, reducing the learning curve associated with a separate templating engine like TwigJs.

5.  **Clearer Component Boundaries:** The `sw-component-section` will act as a boundary to limit the scope of `sw-block-parent` components to their immediate component context, preventing unintended overriding across disparate parts of the application.

**Implementation Details:**

*   **`sw-block` component:**
    *   Accepts a `name` prop (String, required).
    *   Uses a default slot for its base content.
    *   Will internally manage a registry or use Vue's provide/inject to allow `sw-block-parent` components to register their modifications.
    *   When rendered, it will determine if it has been overridden or extended by any `sw-block-parent` within its `sw-component-section` context and render the appropriate content.

*   **`sw-block-parent` component:**
    *   Accepts a `name` prop (String, required), matching the `name` of the `sw-block` to be targeted.
    *   Will have a slot for the content that will override or extend the target `sw-block`.
    *   Will communicate with the corresponding `sw-block` (likely via provide/inject or a global event bus within a section) to deliver its content.
    *   May include props or mechanisms to define *how* the content should be applied (e.g., `mode="override"` or `mode="append"` or `mode="prepend"`).

This decision moves us towards a more unified and modern frontend architecture, fully embracing Vue.js's capabilities for component reusability and extensibility.

To comply with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), we aim to make Shopware 6's document solution accessible (A11y-compliant). This ensures that our solution remains usable while meeting legal requirements and making documents accessible to customers with disabilities.

decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

To ensure Shopware 6's document solution meets Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) and is A11y-compliant, we will replace DomPDF with a new PDF generation library that inherently supports accessibility features. This decision is driven by the following factors:

*   **WCAG Compliance:** Our primary goal is to provide an accessible document solution. The chosen library must support features like tagged PDFs, semantic structure, text equivalents for non-text content, and proper document metadata to meet WCAG standards.
*   **Legal Requirements:** Adhering to WCAG helps us meet legal obligations regarding digital accessibility, reducing potential legal risks and ensuring inclusivity for all users.

## Context
The existing rule system is flexible but complex, making it difficult to evolve and maintain. Allowing unrestricted extensions of rule classes slows down improvements and increases the complexity of the system.

See RFC: https://github.com/shopware/shopware/discussions/5785
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

We want to restrict the extension points for custom rule conditions. This will simplify the rule system, reduce maintenance effort, and make it easier to introduce new features.

Custom rule conditions will be restricted in the following ways:

1.  **No new rule condition classes**: Custom rule conditions can no longer be defined by creating new PHP classes that extend `Shopware\Core\Framework\Rule\Rule`. Instead, app developers will use a generic "script rule" condition.
2.  **Script-based logic**: The logic for custom rule conditions will be implemented using Twig scripts provided by apps. These scripts will be stored in the database and executed within a secure PHP sandbox.
3.  **Manifest-driven configuration**: The configuration for custom rule conditions (e.g., input fields, operators, constraints) will be defined in the app's manifest file. This will allow the administration to render the rule builder dynamically without needing custom Vue components.
4.  **Limited data access**: The Twig scripts will have controlled access to data relevant for rule evaluation, primarily through the `RuleScope` and its available context objects (`Context`, `SalesChannelContext`). Direct database access or arbitrary service calls from scripts will not be allowed.

This approach ensures that custom rule conditions are isolated and do not introduce unintended side effects or performance bottlenecks within the core rule system. It also streamlines the process of adding new conditions by centralizing configuration and logic within the app's definition.

## Context

Currently, flows are executed during the business process. A business
process is any event that is triggered by the user, like a checkout or
a product update. Flows are used to react to these events and execute user defined actions.

There are several downsides to this approach. The most straightforward is the possibility of a fatal error during
the execution of any flow. This will inevitably cancel the in progress business process. While there are remedies in place
to avoid any trivial errors in flow execution disrupting the business process, certain errors can not be avoided.

Further, even if all flows execute without error, they noticeably impact business process performance. Flows are often 
employed to, for example, send mails, an expensive operation that is not necessary to complete the business process.

In addition to these concrete disadvantages, there are also some more abstract ones. For one, currently flows are executed directly
from a decorator of Symfony's `EventDispatcher`, leading to cumbersome debugging and bloated stack traces. This would
be improved if flows are executed by a dedicated event listener. Additionally moving flows to their own execution
environment would not only simplify debugging, but also potentially make expanding their capabilities easier.

> *The following is all experimental and only takes effect if the associated feature flag `FLOW_EXECUTION_AFTER_BUSINESS_PROCESS` is enabled*
decision:
## Decision 
## Decision

Flows will be executed **after** the business process is completed.

This means that instead of directly executing a flow, the flow will be recorded and then executed once the business process completes.
This is accomplished by a dedicated event listener that listens to `kernel.finish_request` and executes any recorded flows at that point.

This approach resolves several of the current issues with flow execution:

*   **No more fatal errors from flows disrupting business processes:** Fatal errors during flow execution will no longer cancel the in progress business process. While the flow will still fail, the user will not experience any disruption to their current task.
*   **Improved business process performance:** Expensive flow operations, such as sending emails, will no longer block the completion of the business process. This will lead to a more responsive user experience.
*   **Simplified debugging and expanded capabilities:** Moving flows to their own execution environment simplifies debugging by providing cleaner stack traces. It also opens up possibilities for future enhancements to flow capabilities, such as asynchronous execution or deferred processing.

This change provides a more robust, performant, and maintainable approach to flow execution, aligning with the goal of separating concerns and improving the overall user experience.

> *This decision only applies when the feature flag `FLOW_EXECUTION_AFTER_BUSINESS_PROCESS` is enabled.*
predicted_decision:
## Decision


We will move the flow execution after the business process. As outlined above we believe that this will simplify the
development around flows, while also improving their performance and safeguarding the main execution environment.

To ensure that flows are executed as close to the business process that triggered them as possible, we will
'queue' the flow execution. This means that flows will be executed after the business process has finished.
Flows are stored in memory and executed as soon as the execution environment signals, that it has
finished a unit of work. The associated events are as follows:

1. After a controller action has been executed (Web) => `KernelEvents::TERMINATE`
2. After a queued message has been processed (Queue) => `WorkerMessageHandledEvent`
3. After a command has been executed (CLI) => `ConsoleEvents::TERMINATE`

Another option would be to handle flow executions as queue messages. This would entirely remove
flow executions from the runtime of the business process. While this would be a simpler solution,
it would both make debugging more complex and introduce an unpredictable delay between the business
process and the flow execution. While this delay could be mitigated by using a high priority queue,
it could not reliably be kept under a certain threshold. To entirely avoid this delay, we decided
that the flow execution should be handled as close to the business process as possible.

## Context and Problem Statement

The Metadata API provides a modern Python API for accessing individual pieces
of metadata. It does not provide any wider context help to someone looking to
implement a TUF repository.

The legacy python-tuf implementation offers tools for this but suffers from
some issues (as do many other implementations):
* There is a _very_ large amount of code to maintain: repo.py,
  repository_tool.py and repository_lib.py alone are almost 7000 lines of code.
* The "library like" parts of the implementation do not form a good coherent
  API: methods routinely have a large number of arguments, code still depends
  on globals in a major way and application (repo.py) still implements a lot of
  "repository code" itself
* The "library like" parts of the implementation make decisions that look like
  application decisions. As an example, repository_tool loads _every_ metadata
  file in the repository: this is fine for CLI that operates on a small
  repository but is unlikely to be a good choice for a large scale server.
decision:
## Decision

The new `Repository` API provides classes and interfaces for implementing TUF
repositories. The key parts of the API are:

* **Repository:** A single class that represents a TUF repository. It holds
  a `StorageBackend` instance and a `KeyStore` instance and provides all the
  methods needed to create and modify a repository.
* **StorageBackend:** An interface for reading and writing metadata and target
  files. Multiple implementations are provided, including ones for local disk
  and in-memory storage.
* **KeyStore:** An interface for managing signing keys. Multiple
  implementations are provided, including ones for local disk and in-memory
  storage.

This design enables developers to implement TUF repositories using a clear and
well-defined API. It also promotes code reusability and reduces the amount of
code that needs to be maintained.

### Advantages

* **Clear and coherent API:** The `Repository` class provides a single entry
  point for all repository operations, making it easier to understand and use.
* **Separation of concerns:** `StorageBackend` and `KeyStore` abstract away
  the details of storage and key management, allowing developers to choose the
  implementations that best suit their needs.
* **Reduced code complexity:** The new API is designed to be concise and
  focused, reducing the overall code footprint.
* **Flexibility:** Developers can easily switch between different storage and
  key management implementations without changing their core repository logic.

### Disadvantages

* **Migration effort:** Existing `python-tuf` users will need to update their
  code to use the new API. This is, however, a necessary step given the issues
  with the legacy implementation.

## Decision Drivers

* There is a consensus on removing the legacy code from python-tuf due to
  maintainability issues
* Metadata API makes modifying metadata far easier than legacy code base: this
  makes significantly different designs possible
* Not providing a "repository library" (and leaving implementers on their own)
  may be a short term solution because of the previous point, but to make
  adoption easier and to help adopters create safe implementations the project
  would benefit from some shared repository code and a shared repository design 
* Maintainability of new library code must be a top concern
* Allowing a wide range of repository implementations (from CLI tools to
  minimal in-memory implementations to large scale application servers)
  would be good: unfortunately these can have wildly differing requirements

## Context

Primer React components was originally released without TypeScript type definitions, making it difficult for engineers to consume the library in TypeScript applications. In [July 2019](https://github.com/primer/react/commit/2983c935ea9ad600c04078adb25e40c3624c11fa#diff-7aa4473ede4abd9ec099e87fec67fd57afafaf39e05d493ab4533acc38547eb8), we created an [ambient declaration](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/typescript-ambients-declaration/) file (`index.d.ts`) file to provide type definitions for TypeScript applications without having to rewrite Primer React components in TypeScript.

`index.d.ts` has been an effective stopgap, enabling teams to build complex applications with Primer React components and TypeScript. However, because `index.d.ts` is disconnected from the implementation code, we've struggled to keep the type definitions up-to-date and accurate, as evidenced by [many](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/906) [TypeScript](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/540) [bug](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/520) [reports](https://github.com/primer/react/issues/534). As the library continues to grow in size and complexity, manually maintaining type definitions will become unsustainable.
